title: Sticks and Stones Can Break My Bones, and Research-Free Reading Routines Can Hurt My Students
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos, a K-3 teacher turned reading specialist, responds to a hostile message from a Structured Word Inquiry practitioner by arguing that early reading instruction must rest on research rather than on appeals to the truth of the writing system. She quotes a ten-point set of SWI prescriptions and notes that none is backed by cited evidence. She then marshals Seidenberg, Share, Dehaene, Ouellette and Sénéchal, and Chall to defend an alphabetic-principle-first approach for beginners, with morphology layered in later. Her wider point is that intuition and vivid experience are not substitutes for systematic evidence, and that new teachers need simple, effective routines. It fits Learning & Curriculum as literacy-instruction pedagogy grounded in research.
points: Janetos holds that unsupported claims about how to teach beginning reading, however principled, are no basis for classroom decisions.
She cites encoding research to argue that writing and decoding reinforce phonemic awareness and the alphabetic principle in early reading.
Her critique of SWI is that overreliance on intuition leads to assertions about starting with morphology that are never checked against evidence.
She stresses that K-1 time is limited, so methods that delay decoding practice carry a real opportunity cost for beginning readers.
New teachers, in her view, need simple and efficient reading routines, not exploratory inquiry that supplants the alphabetic principle.
quotes: Bad things happen when we eschew it and just start making stuff up with suppositions about how something might work (or ought to work) because it comports with companionable, yet untested, theories and enticing philosophies. I have pointed out in both SWI blogs the selective hearing among some SWI practitioners that results in disassociating with the research—they either ignore it or just cherry-pick the choice bits.
Phonics instruction is foundational. The evidence is clear that learning how the writing system works—particularly how spellings map onto sounds—is essential for becoming a skilled reader.

Compelling research by Ouellette and Sénéchal shows how encoding—turning what we say into something we see—reinforces phonemic awareness, which in turn improves reading. This research on the importance of fostering PA by linking phonemes with graphemes supports the reciprocal nature of reading and writing and emphasizes the crucial role of the alphabetic principle in beginning reading instruction.

An overreliance on intuition definitely plagues the SWI community and leads to assertions that have some version of this statement: Starting with morphology must be the best place to start since it aligns with the truth of our writing system. This assertion seems intuitive to these advocates.

The choices we K-1 teachers make should be the ones that research—yes, research—has shown to be effective—and then confirmed by our practice. Teaching decoding is not part of a devotional. Our respect for the alphabetic principle isn’t based on reverence for the language.

Sure—we like our English language a lot. It serves us well. But we are in the business of servicing an entire class of beginning readers, many of whom come to us having had few literacy-rich experiences, and we choose methods that work with—not against—their brains.
